### C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

107. **The numerator set M(p) is divisor-closed, so ES ⇔ M(p) contains a multiple of 4** [`analogues-0107`; high/cheap] — Let M(p) = {m : m/p is a sum of three unit fractions}. If m/p = Σ 1/x_i and d | m then (m/d)/p = Σ 1/(d x_i), so M(p) is closed under divisors. Hence ES(p) ⇔ 4k ∈ M(p) for some k ≥ 1. — *First step:* For p ≤ 10^5 compute M(p) (from all 3-term representations with any numerator) and record which element divisible by 4 appears first; look for a large-m element that is forced (like p + 1 ∈ M(p) always).
108. **Forced elements of M(p): p + 1, p + 2, 2p + ... — which large numerators are always available?** [`analogues-0108`; high/cheap] — (p+1)/p = 1 + 1/(2p) + 1/(2p) shows p + 1 ∈ M(p); similarly (p+2)/p = 1 + 1/p + 1/p and 3 ∈ M(p). A large forced element divisible by 4 would prove ES via divisor-closure. — *First step:* Enumerate polynomial families m(p) = ap + b with uniform identities (b small) and list their m mod 4 for p ≡ 1 mod 4; check whether all forced ones are ≢ 0 mod 4 (T1-type).
109. **All-even ES ⇔ 8/p is a sum of three unit fractions: fails at p = 17, 241 (p < 4000)** [`analogues-0109`; high/cheap] — Denominators all even ⇔ 8/p = Σ 1/(x_i/2). In the computation, 'all even' fails only at p = 17 and 241 among 269 primes p ≡ 1 mod 4 below 4000. Schinzel's conjecture for m = 8 predicts finitely many failures. — *First step:* Done to 2·10^4 (data/z52b/analogues_constraints_20000.txt: still only 17, 241 among 1125 primes). Extend to 10^6 with a faster search and compare with known Schinzel m = 8 data.
110. **'Some denominator ≡ 0 mod 4' fails at exactly the same primes 17, 241 as m = 8** [`analogues-0110`; high/cheap] — Among p < 4000 the solutions with a denominator divisible by 4 are missing exactly at p = 17 and 241, the same primes where 8/p fails. A structural equivalence (e.g. a bijection of solution types) may lie behind this. — *First step:* Failure sets coincide (= {17, 241}) up to 2·10^4 as well (data/z52b/analogues_constraints_20000.txt). Try to prove: if 4 | x in 4/p = Σ 1/x_i, then a solution of 8/p can be produced (and conversely).
111. **Norm denominators: all x, y, z sums of two squares — fails at 16 primes below 4000** [`analogues-0111`; med/cheap] — Requiring every denominator to be a norm from Z[i] (sum of two squares) fails at p = 41, 137, 233, 241, 601, 769, … (16 of 269). This is the 'Gaussian-norm' constrained world. — *First step:* Up to 2·10^4: 40 failures among 1125 primes (data/z52b/analogues_constraints_20000.txt). Test whether failures are density-zero, and check whether a local obstruction (e.g. mod 8 or mod 3) explains them.
112. **Chain constraint x | y | z: fails at 38 of 269 primes below 4000** [`analogues-0112`; med/cheap] — 4/p = (1/x)(1 + 1/a + 1/(ab)) with y = ax, z = abx. The chain world is a 3-parameter subfamily; failures start at p = 73, 193, 313, 337. — *First step:* (161 failures among 1125 primes below 2·10^4.) Characterize: x | y | z ⇔ p·(ab + b + 1) = 4abx; derive the congruence conditions on p and compare with the failure list.
113. **z is a common multiple of x and y: fails only at p = 2521 below 4000** [`analogues-0113`; high/cheap] — Solutions with x | z and y | z exist for every p ≡ 1 mod 4 below 4000 except 2521. This sub-world is almost as rich as ES. — *First step:* Still only 2521 below 2·10^4 (data/z52b/analogues_constraints_20000.txt). Parametrize lcm-solutions (z = lcm) explicitly and run to 10^6 to see if exceptions stay sparse; inspect 2521 = 2521 (prime) for special structure.
114. **Odd-denominator ES is impossible (2-adic): the archetype of a constrained-world local obstruction** [`analogues-0114`; high/cheap] — If x, y, z are odd, xy + yz + zx is odd and xyz odd, so the reduced fraction has odd numerator, while 4/n (n odd) has numerator 4. So no solution. Likewise exactly one even denominator is impossible by 2-adic valuations (the computation confirms). — *First step:* Generalize: for which multiplicative sets H ⊂ (Z/ℓ^k)^* of allowed denominator classes is there a local obstruction? Tabulate for ℓ ≤ 7.
115. **Denominators ≡ 1 (mod 3) is impossible when 3 ∤ n: a 3-adic obstruction** [`analogues-0115`; high/cheap] — If x, y, z ≡ 1 mod 3 then 1/x + 1/y + 1/z ≡ 3 ≡ 0 in Z_(3), while 4/n is a 3-adic unit when 3 ∤ n. More generally, with k terms and denominators ≡ 1 mod ℓ, one needs 4/n ≡ k (mod ℓ). — *First step:* Tabulate for ℓ ∈ {3,5,7}, H = subgroup of (Z/ℓ)^*, the classes of n for which ES_H is locally obstructed.
116. **Pairwise coprime denominators: impossible for n ≥ 2** [`analogues-0116`; high/cheap] — If gcd(x,y) = gcd(y,z) = gcd(x,z) = 1, the fraction (xy+yz+zx)/xyz is already reduced, so xyz = n·t and xy + yz + zx = 4t with t = 1, impossible for positive integers. All solutions need shared factors among denominators. — *First step:* Count, for p < 4000, solutions with exactly one coprime pair vs none (the computation shows 'all pairs share a factor' never fails).
117. **Squarefree denominators: never fails for p < 4000 — conjecture ES with squarefree x, y, z** [`analogues-0117`; med/cheap] — The constrained world 'all denominators squarefree' had a solution at every p ≡ 1 mod 4 below 4000 (also cube-free, pairwise non-coprime, distinct). — *First step:* Extend to 10^6 (cheap with a smarter search); if no failures, formulate 'ES_sqf' and check how Type II parameters (a,b,c,d) must look for squarefree output.
118. **At least one denominator prime: fails at 93 of 269 primes below 4000** [`analogues-0118`; high/cheap] — Requiring some denominator to be prime (often p itself, i.e. 3/p = 1/y + 1/z) fails frequently: p = 37, 73, 97, 193, …. With x = p it is the 2-term problem 3/p = 1/y + 1/z, solvable iff p has... (p prime: iff p ≡ 2 mod 3). — *First step:* Check: failures ⊆ {p ≡ 1 mod 3}? and the remaining prime-denominator solutions with a prime ≠ p — classify.
119. **Arithmetic-progression denominators x, y, z in AP never occur (p < 4000)** [`analogues-0119`; med/cheap] — No solution with y − x = z − y appears for any p. Possibly a provable impossibility (or extreme rarity) via the equation 4x(x+d)(x+2d) = p(…) — *First step:* Write 4/p = 1/x + 1/(x+d) + 1/(x+2d) as a cubic curve in (x, d) and test for rational points; check whether a local obstruction rules it out.
120. **Sierpiński 5/n: the m = 5 twin of ES (verified to 10^18 per Pomerance's notes)** [`analogues-0120`; high/cheap] — 5/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z is open in exactly the same way: almost-all (Vaughan) and polynomial identities except square classes. Comparing hard classes of m = 4 and m = 5 separates numerator-specific from universal obstructions. — *First step:* Compute the mod-M uncovered classes for m = 5 after all small Type I/II identities (like Mordell's 840 for m = 4) and compare with T1 squares.
121. **Schinzel's m/n conjecture: table of the largest exception N(m) for m ≤ 30** [`analogues-0121`; high/cheap] — For each m, compute the n for which m/n is not a 3-term sum. Schinzel conjectures finiteness for each m. The growth of N(m) in m is the 'numerator direction' of the phase diagram. — *First step:* Brute force m ≤ 30, n ≤ 10^5; record N(m) and exception counts; check literature for existing tables (e.g. Guy UPINT D11).
122. **Mordell–Schinzel for general m: are square classes obstructed for every numerator?** [`analogues-0122`; high/medium] — For m = 4 square classes mod M admit no polynomial identities. Check whether the same holds for every m (and whether additional obstructed classes appear for composite m such as 8 or 12). — *First step:* Run the identity-coverage search for m = 5..12 modulo 840·k and list uncovered classes; compare with squares.
123. **Numerator ladder 4 | 8 | 16 | …: ES(4·2^j) ⇒ ES(4) and exceptions grow with j** [`analogues-0123`; med/cheap] — By divisor-closure, 2^{j+2}/p solvable ⇒ 4/p solvable. The exceptional sets E_j for m = 2^{j+2} grow with j; ES ⇔ E_0 = ∅. Data at j = 1 (m = 8): {17, 241} below 4000. — *First step:* Compute E_1, E_2 (m = 8, 16) for p < 10^5 and check whether hard ES primes (few solutions, e.g. 5, 13, 17, 193) are in all E_j.
124. **Two-term criterion (a/n = 1/x + 1/y) as the solved sub-world: the e-slice reduces ES to it** [`analogues-0124`; high/cheap] — a/n = 1/x + 1/y ⇔ n·(stuff) has a divisor in a residue class (Rav-type criterion). ES ⇔ for some x, (4x − n)/(nx) satisfies the 2-term criterion. So ES is a union over x of solved problems. — *First step:* Write the exact 2-term criterion and express #ES-solutions(p) as Σ_x (#divisors of (nx)² in a class mod (4x − n)); compare with the repo's Type I/II counts.
125. **Huang–Vaughan exceptional set asymptotic for a/n = 1/x+1/y → model for ES exceptions in a single slice** [`analogues-0125`; high/medium] — Huang–Vaughan prove E_a(N) ~ C(a) N (log log N)^{2^{m−1}−1}/(log N)^{1−1/2^m} for fixed a, via 'delicate analysis of the underlying group structure' ((Z/aZ)^* and subgroups). ES needs a union over slices a = 4x − n with x varying. — *First step:* Read Huang–Vaughan's method and identify whether it extends to 'for some a in a set A(n)' with A depending on n (union bound + correlation).
126. **One numerator-2 term trivializes ES: 4/n = 2/((n+1)/2) + 1/M + 1/M, M = n(n+1)/2** [`analogues-0126`; high/cheap] — For odd n: 4/n − 4/(n+1) = 4/(n(n+1)) = 2/M = 1/M + 1/M with M = n(n+1)/2. So allowing a single term with numerator 2 (and a repeat) solves every odd n. — *First step:* Record as a lemma; then explore weight vectors (1,1,1) vs (1,1,2) vs (1,2,3) for distinct denominators.
127. **Weighted ES: 4/n = a/x + b/y + c/z for fixed weight vectors (a,b,c)** [`analogues-0127`; high/cheap] — A whole family of ternary problems indexed by (a,b,c). (1,1,2) is trivial (previous item); (1,1,1) is ES. Which weight vectors are 'hard' (lottery) vs 'trivial' (identity covering) vs 'false'? — *First step:* Brute-force n ≤ 10^4 for all (a,b,c) with a,b,c ≤ 4 and classify by existence of a finite covering by identities mod 840.
128. **Signed ES with a size-controlled negative term: 4/n = 1/x + 1/y − 1/z with z ≥ n^{1+δ}** [`analogues-0128`; med/cheap] — Signed ES is trivial (4/(4k+1) = 1/k − 1/(k(4k+1))). Requiring the negative term to be tiny (z large) interpolates between trivial and ES-like. Find the threshold δ at which signed ES stops being covered by identities. — *First step:* For p ≤ 10^4, compute the maximal z over signed solutions with one negative term; check whether z ≥ p³ is always achievable (via identities).
129. **Best underapproximation of 4/n by three unit fractions (Kovač / Nathanson / Chu) — ES ⇔ gap 0** [`analogues-0129`; med/cheap] — The 'best k-term underapproximation' literature studies max{Σ_{i≤k} 1/x_i ≤ q}. ES ⇔ the 3-term underapproximation of 4/n is exact. Structure theorems for best underapproximations (eventually greedy) might constrain when exactness is possible. — *First step:* Read Kovač 2406.07218 and Nathanson 2202.00191; compute the best 3-term underapproximation of 4/p for p ≤ 10^4 and check whether greedy first term works.
130. **Odd greedy algorithm (open termination problem) ↔ odd-denominator Egyptian fractions** [`analogues-0130`; med/cheap] — Every rational with odd denominator is a finite sum of distinct odd unit fractions (Breusch / Stewart, to check), but whether the odd greedy algorithm terminates is a famous open problem. ES with odd denominators is impossible (2-adic), but 4/n with an even number ≥ 4 of odd terms is a natural neighbour. — *First step:* Check the status of the odd greedy problem and of 'minimal number of odd unit fractions for 4/n' (must be even ≥ 4 by parity); compute for n ≤ 1000.
131. **Minimal number of odd unit fractions for 4/n: parity forces an even count ≥ 4** [`analogues-0131`; high/cheap] — A sum of k odd unit fractions has numerator Σ_i Π_{j≠i} x_j ≡ k (mod 2) over an odd denominator; since 4/n (n odd) has even numerator, k must be EVEN. Hence 4/n with odd denominators needs an even number of terms ≥ 4. — *First step:* Compute for n ≤ 10^4 (n odd) whether 4/n is a sum of four odd unit fractions; look for obstructions mod 8.
132. **Shifted-prime denominators (Bloom): 4/n with denominators of the form q − 1, q prime** [`analogues-0132`; med/cheap] — Bloom proved results on unit fractions with shifted prime denominators (density/Ramsey type). The 3-term restriction 4/n = Σ 1/(q_i − 1) is a sparse constrained world. — *First step:* Compute the expected number of solutions under the lottery model and compare with brute force for n ≤ 10^4.
133. **Semiprime denominators: 4/p as a sum of three reciprocals of semiprimes** [`analogues-0133`; med/cheap] — Recent work shows every natural number is a sum of distinct semiprime unit fractions (Shisheng Li). The 3-term version for 4/p is a constrained ES with a natural density of allowed denominators ~ log log x / log x. — *First step:* Brute force for p ≤ 10^4; record failure density; compare with lottery prediction.
134. **Denominators in short intervals (Croot) ↔ size windows for ES solutions** [`analogues-0134`; med/cheap] — Croot studied unit fractions with denominators in short intervals [N, N + N^θ]. ES solutions have x ∈ (p/4, 3p/4] and y, z in structured ranges; asking for all three denominators in a short window is a size-constrained world. — *First step:* Read Croot math/9904181 to see whether his argument has a 3-term component; compute the window widths of ES solutions for hard primes.
135. **Rado/partition regularity of 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/w** [`analogues-0135`; med/cheap] — Brown–Rödl-type results transfer Rado's theorem to reciprocal equations. Is 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/w partition regular (monochromatic x, y, z, w in any finite colouring)? The linear counterpart x + y + z = 4w is not regular (no zero subset-sum of coefficients), but reciprocal equations can behave differently. — *First step:* Check the reciprocal Rado literature (Brown–Rödl; Gaiser 2306.04029) for 1/x+1/y+1/z = c/w; try 2-colourings by computer for small ranges.
136. **Covering systems ↔ unit fractions (Z.-W. Sun): ES as a statement about AP packings** [`analogues-0136`; high/cheap] — Sun relates m-covers by residue classes to sums of unit fractions of moduli. Three pairwise disjoint APs with moduli x, y, z have density Σ 1/x_i; ES ⇔ some disjoint triple of APs has density exactly 4/n (disjointness needs pairwise gcd > 1, which every ES solution has). — *First step:* Prove the equivalence 'ES ⇔ disjoint AP triple of density 4/n' and check whether every ES solution's moduli admit disjoint residues (pairwise gcd > 1 suffices).
137. **Elsholtz–Planitzer approximate parametrizations for k ≥ 4 unit fractions** [`analogues-0137`; high/cheap] — For sums of four and more unit fractions, Elsholtz–Planitzer use approximate parametrizations to count solutions. ES is the k = 3 case where exact parametrizations (Type I/II) exist. — *First step:* Read arXiv:2012.05984 and 1805.02945; check whether any pointwise (fixed n) 4-term statement is proved.
138. **Four-term ES with distinct denominators is trivial — but four-term with a size cap is not** [`analogues-0138`; med/cheap] — 4/n as a sum of 4 unit fractions is easy (e.g. via 3/n splitting). With all denominators ≤ C·n (no huge denominators), the 4-term problem becomes a lattice/lottery problem again. — *First step:* Compute, for n ≤ 10^4, the least C such that 4/n has a 4-term representation with max denominator ≤ C n; test boundedness.
139. **Distinctness is harmless: the 'distinct' world never fails (p < 4000)** [`analogues-0139`; high/cheap] — Every p ≡ 1 mod 4 below 4000 has a solution with x, y, z distinct. Folklore says distinctness is WLOG for n > 2. — *First step:* Write the splitting lemma: if x = y then 2/x = 1/(x/2)... or use 1/x = 1/(x+1) + 1/(x(x+1)) with care to keep 3 terms; check the literature statement.
140. **A₃(p)-numerator geometry: the set M(p) as lattice points under a hyperbola** [`analogues-0140`; med/cheap] — m ∈ M(p) iff m/p = Σ 1/x_i; for each Type II parameter set, the achievable m form arithmetic progressions. M(p) is then a union of APs intersected with [1, 3p]. — *First step:* For p ≤ 10^4 compute M(p) and fit it as a union of APs; inspect the differences mod 4.
141. **Egyptian fractions with restricted prime support (Chen–Elsholtz–Jiang; Czenky–McGovern–Plavnik)** [`analogues-0141`; high/cheap] — Representations of 1 with denominators in S(p_1,…,p_t) (S-units) are studied; ES in Z[1/S] relates. For ES over ℕ with denominators S-smooth except for factors of p, the count is finite and computable. — *First step:* For S = {2,3,5,7}, enumerate solutions of 4/p = Σ 1/x_i with x_i ∈ p^{0,1}·S-units, p ≤ 10^6; find which p are covered.
142. **4/n as a sum of three reciprocals of squares (Graham-type world)** [`analogues-0142`; med/cheap] — Graham characterized rationals that are finite sums of reciprocals of distinct squares. The 3-term version 4/n = 1/a² + 1/b² + 1/c² is a sparse world with local obstructions. — *First step:* Compute for n ≤ 10^5 which n admit 4/n = Σ 1/a_i² (3 terms) and look for congruence patterns.
143. **Mixed: 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z² (one square denominator)** [`analogues-0143`; low/cheap] — One square denominator keeps the problem 2-dimensional but couples to quadratic residues. It is a sibling where the T1 square obstruction might be amplified or cancelled. — *First step:* Brute force n ≤ 10^4; for each solvable n record the class of z mod small primes.
144. **ES with denominators restricted to a numerical semigroup or to values of a polynomial** [`analogues-0144`; low/cheap] — E.g. denominators of the form k(k+1) (pronic) telescope: 1/(k(k+1)) = 1/k − 1/(k+1). ES with pronic denominators is a strongly restricted world with a telescoping algebra. — *First step:* Brute force n ≤ 10^4 for pronic and triangular denominators; derive the equivalence with signed sums.
145. **Distinct-odd unit fraction representations: every odd-denominator rational is a finite sum (to check: Breusch 1954, Stewart 1954)** [`analogues-0145`; med/cheap] — If verified, this is the 'unbounded-length odd' world where existence is known; ES's length-3 even-structured requirement is the opposite extreme. — *First step:* Check whether Breusch/Stewart give explicit length bounds; compute minimal odd lengths for 4/n, n ≤ 1000.
146. **Rational numbers representable with three unit fractions: density among a/b with b ≤ N** [`analogues-0146`; med/cheap] — Most rationals a/b with a large are not 3-term sums. ES says all 4/n are. Placing 4/n in the 2D picture (a, b) shows ES is on a 'ray' where the density is 1 conjecturally. — *First step:* Compute, for b ≤ 2000, the proportion of representable a/b as a function of a; plot transition.
147. **ES restricted to 'Type I only' or 'Type II only': two sub-worlds with known almost-all behaviour** [`analogues-0147`; high/cheap] — Elsholtz–Tao distinguish Type I (p divides one denominator) and Type II (p divides two). Each sub-world is a constrained ES; which primes need Type II? (Computation: 'y, z both divisible by p' never fails below 4000; 'only z divisible by p' never fails either.) — *First step:* Extend to 10^6: does 'Type II only' (p | y, p | z) ever fail? (Repo has censuses—check I3/Type II data first.)
148. **Greedy/Fibonacci–Sylvester world: 4/n has ≤ 4 greedy terms; ES needs 3** [`analogues-0148`; high/cheap] — The greedy algorithm on 4/n terminates in at most 4 terms (numerators decrease). The classes where greedy gives 3 terms are covered; ES fails for greedy at others but other expansions work. — *First step:* Implement 'greedy with first term chosen from {⌈n/4⌉ + j : j ≤ J}' and find the least J(p) for which the remainder is a 2-term sum; study J(p) growth.
149. **ES for numerators m that are prime vs composite (4 composite, 5 prime)** [`analogues-0149`; low/cheap] — Divisor-closure links composite numerators to their divisors; a prime numerator m has no proper non-trivial divisor (except 1). Compare exception structures across prime and composite m. — *First step:* Using the Schinzel table item, compare exception counts for m prime vs composite at fixed n-range.
150. **Egyptian fractions on topological groups (Ross): ES in the circle group or in Q_p** [`analogues-0150`; low/cheap] — Ross extends structure results on sets of Egyptian fractions to subsets of topological groups. An ES analogue in R/Z or Q_p asks which elements are 3-term sums from a discrete generating set. — *First step:* Read arXiv:2410.24165 to see which structure theorems carry over and whether derived-set orders give constraints on 4/n.
151. **Derived-set (accumulation) structure: 4/n is never an accumulation point of 3-term sums except via 2-term limits** [`analogues-0151`; low/cheap] — The set E₃ of 3-term sums is closed with accumulation points in E₂ (2-term sums). 4/n ∈ E₃ is a statement about an isolated vs limit point. — *First step:* Compute dist(4/p, E₃ ∖ {4/p}) for p ≤ 10^4 and compare with the expected spacing.
152. **Engel and Pierce expansions: ES as a length-3 Engel-type representation** [`analogues-0152`; med/cheap] — Chain solutions (x | y | z) are Engel-like (1/x(1 + 1/a(1 + 1/b))). Engel/Pierce expansions of 4/n are deterministic; their lengths give a dynamical invariant. — *First step:* Compute the Engel expansion length of 4/p for p ≤ 10^5; correlate with chain-world failures (38 below 4000).

### D. Geometric, topological and combinatorial host worlds

153. **Triangle orbifolds: ES ⇔ 4/n − 1 is the Euler characteristic of a turnover S²(x,y,z)** [`analogues-0153`; high/cheap] — χ^orb(S²(x,y,z)) = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z − 1. So ES(n) ⇔ some hyperbolic triangle orbifold has χ = (4 − n)/n, i.e. area 2π(1 − 4/n). — *First step:* Check whether 'areas of hyperbolic triangle orbifolds' as a set of rationals has been studied (search 'orbifold Euler characteristic triangle group which rationals'); list areas for arithmetic triangle groups.
154. **Riemann–Hurwitz integrality: a surface subgroup of Δ(x,y,z) of index d needs n | d(n − 4)** [`analogues-0154`; med/medium] — For an ES solution, a torsion-free normal subgroup of index d in Δ(x,y,z) yields genus g with 2g − 2 = d(1 − 4/n). Hence n must divide d(n − 4); for prime n ≥ 5 this forces n | d. — *First step:* For small n list ES triples and check whether PSL₂(F_p) is a quotient of Δ(x,y,z) (Macbeath's criterion); see if a uniform choice like PSL₂(F_p) suggests a construction.
155. **Brieskorn–Pham log canonical thresholds: ES ⇔ 4/n = lct(x^a + y^b + z^c)** [`analogues-0155`; high/cheap] — For the diagonal singularity x^a + y^b + z^c, lct = min(1, 1/a + 1/b + 1/c). So ES(n) ⇔ 4/n (< 1 for n ≥ 5) is the log canonical threshold of a 3-variable Brieskorn–Pham polynomial. — *First step:* Check the known description of LCT for quasi-homogeneous isolated singularities in 3 variables (Arnold's types) and list which rationals arise from each type.
156. **Quasi-homogeneous relaxations: lct of x^a y + y^b + z^c is (a + b − 1)/(ab) + 1/c** [`analogues-0156`; med/cheap] — For f = x^a y + y^b + z^c, weights w_y = 1/b, w_x = (b − 1)/(ab), w_z = 1/c give lct = Σ w = (a+b−1)/(ab) + 1/c (if ≤ 1). Each Arnold/Orlik–Wagreich type gives a 'generalized Egyptian' expression for rationals. — *First step:* Derive the weight-sum formulas for the 7 Orlik–Wagreich-type classes of 3-variable isolated quasi-homogeneous singularities and test which represent 4/p for all p ≤ 10^4.
157. **Brieskorn links: ES solutions never give integral homology spheres** [`analogues-0157`; med/cheap] — The link of x^a + y^b + z^c is an integral homology sphere iff a, b, c are pairwise coprime. Pairwise coprime ES solutions are impossible (constraint-world item), so ES links always have non-trivial H₁. — *First step:* Compute H₁ of Brieskorn links for ES triples of small p and compare with the Type I/II parameters.
158. **Seifert fibred spaces: ES ⇔ M(0; (x,1), (y,1), (z,1)) has rational Euler number −4/n** [`analogues-0158`; med/cheap] — For a Seifert space over S² with unnormalized invariants (α_i, β_i) = (x_i, 1) and b = 0, e = −Σ β_i/α_i = −(1/x + 1/y + 1/z). So ES ⇔ such a space has e = −4/n, and then |H₁| = xyz·|e| = 4xyz/n = xy + yz + zx. — *First step:* Check: a fibre-preserving d-fold cover of M multiplies e by a rational factor; derive which covers map ES(n) solutions to ES(n') solutions.
159. **Pretzel links: det P(x,y,z) = xy + yz + zx = 4xyz/n for ES triples** [`analogues-0159`; med/cheap] — The pretzel link P(x,y,z) has determinant |xy + yz + zx| (its double branched cover is the Seifert space above). ES ⇔ some pretzel link with positive parameters has det·n = 4·xyz. — *First step:* For ES triples of small p compute signature and Alexander polynomial of P(x,y,z); look for constraints that would forbid solutions at specific p.
160. **Star-shaped Dynkin trees T_{x,y,z}: det(Cartan) = xyz(1/x + 1/y + 1/z − 1)** [`analogues-0160`; med/cheap] — The tree T_{p,q,r} (arms with p, q, r vertices including the centre) has Cartan determinant pqr(1/p+1/q+1/r − 1) (E₈ = T_{2,3,5}: 1; E₆ = T_{2,3,3}: 3). ES ⇔ some T_{x,y,z} has n·det = xyz(4 − n), a hyperbolic lattice of discriminant xyz(n−4)/n. — *First step:* Compute discriminant groups of T_{x,y,z} lattices for ES triples of small p; see whether they have a uniform structure (e.g. cyclic of order xyz(n−4)/n).
161. **Weighted star trees with central weight k: generalized ES 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z − (k − 2)** [`analogues-0161`; low/cheap] — Torrente-Lujan allows central diagonal entry k; the determinant becomes xyz(Σ 1/x_i − (k − 1)) up to normalization (check the exact formula). Different k shift the target by integers, giving 'ES with integer offset'. — *First step:* Read arXiv:2605.23011 for the determinant formula with general k and record the induced Egyptian equation.
162. **Parallel resistors: ES ⇔ a resistance n/4 Ω made from three integer resistors in parallel** [`analogues-0162`; high/cheap] — Conductances add in parallel: 1/R = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z. So ES ⇔ R = n/4 is a parallel combination of three integer resistors (equivalently three thin lenses of integer focal length in contact). — *First step:* Check the literature on 'realizing resistance values with k resistors' (series–parallel, minimal number of unit resistors) for 3-branch parallel results.
163. **Rectangle tilings: ES ⇔ an n×4 rectangle split into three horizontal strips, each a row of equal squares** [`analogues-0163`; med/cheap] — A strip of width W tiled by x equal squares has height W/x; three strips stacked give height W(1/x+1/y+1/z). Thus ES(n) ⇔ the rectangle of aspect n : 4 is tiled by three such strips. — *First step:* Formalize and check whether allowing strips to be split further (two-level tilings) yields a known Dehn-type characterization that ES is a restriction of.
164. **Perfectly periodic schedules: three tasks with periods x, y, z sharing a slot pattern of density 4/n** [`analogues-0164`; med/cheap] — A perfectly periodic schedule assigns task i to an AP of period x_i, all disjoint. ES ⇔ three disjoint APs of total density 4/n exist. Pinwheel scheduling (Kawamura: density threshold 5/6 proved) studies the non-exact version. — *First step:* Read Kawamura's density-threshold proof to see if exact-density perfectly periodic schedules with three tasks are characterized.
165. **Kraft–McMillan / compact trees ↔ sums of unit fractions (Elsholtz–Heuberger–Prodinger)** [`analogues-0165`; low/cheap] — Compact prefix codes and canonical trees are counted via sums of unit fractions; ES-type identities appear as specific tree shapes with three leaves of weights 1/x_i summing to 4/n. — *First step:* Read arXiv:1108.5964 to see which unit-fraction equations correspond to which trees; check whether 3-leaf subtrees encode ES.
166. **Landau's class equation and fusion-category Egyptian equations: 1 = Σ 1/|C(g_i)|** [`analogues-0166`; low/cheap] — Integral modular categories and finite groups yield Egyptian equations for 1 (Landau; Bruillard–Rowell). A group with 4 conjugacy classes gives 1 − 1/|G| = three unit fractions, an ES-type equation with numerator |G| − 1. — *First step:* Enumerate (N−1)/N = 1/a + 1/b + 1/c solutions and compare with groups having 4 classes (Z₄, V₄, D₅, A₄); note which equations are 'realized'.
167. **Hirzebruch–Jung continued fractions and cyclic quotient singularities ↔ ES₅** [`analogues-0167`; med/cheap] — ES₅ (continued-fraction length ≤ 3) can be read as a statement about cyclic quotient singularities 1/p(1, q) whose HJ continued fraction (resolution graph) has a specific short shape. — *First step:* Translate λ(p) ≤ 3 into an HJ-continued-fraction condition on some q mod p and check against bsA_toric_ksb_wahl.md.
168. **Dessins d'enfants of type (x, y, z): Belyi maps whose ramification orders are an ES triple** [`analogues-0168`; low/medium] — A regular dessin of type (x,y,z) with N darts has χ = N(1/x+1/y+1/z − 1). ES triples give dessins with χ/N = 4/n − 1; the Galois action on such dessins is a new (arithmetic) structure on ES solutions. — *First step:* Compute fields of moduli of the smallest regular dessins with ES types for p = 5, 13, 17 (via PSL₂ quotients).
169. **Arithmetic triangle groups (Takeuchi's 85) and ES triples** [`analogues-0169`; med/cheap] — Only finitely many triangle groups are arithmetic (Takeuchi). An ES triple (x,y,z) giving an arithmetic Δ would carry a quaternion algebra; for large n, ES triples are non-arithmetic. — *First step:* List Takeuchi's 85 triples, compute 1/x+1/y+1/z, and find which equal 4/n.
170. **Spherical / Euclidean / hyperbolic trichotomy as a 'phase diagram' of numerators** [`analogues-0170`; high/cheap] — 1/x + 1/y + 1/z > 1 (spherical, finite list), = 1 (Euclidean: (3,3,3),(2,4,4),(2,3,6)), < 1 (hyperbolic). ES with 4/n < 1 sits in the hyperbolic regime; numerators m/n > 1 give the finite spherical lists. — *First step:* Record as context; check whether 'which rationals in (1, 3] are 3-term sums' (finite-ish lists per denominator) gives a useful contrast for heuristics.
171. **Tessellations and Wythoff constructions: uniform tilings with vertex configurations from ES triples** [`analogues-0171`; low/cheap] — A triangle (π/x, π/y, π/z) tiles the hyperbolic plane; vertex/edge/face counts of Wythoff tilings depend on 1/x+1/y+1/z. ES triples give tilings with angle defect 2π·... proportional to (1 − 4/n). — *First step:* Low priority: note equivalence; compute angle defects of ES triangles for p ≤ 100.
172. **Hurwitz existence problem for branched covers with three branch points** [`analogues-0172`; low/cheap] — A degree-N cover of S² branched over 3 points with all ramification orders x, y, z respectively (uniform data) exists iff Riemann–Hurwitz integrality holds plus combinatorial conditions; for ES triples the data have χ = N(4/n − 1). — *First step:* Formulate 'ES with averaged reciprocals' (branch data with different ramification orders above each point) and check if it is always solvable.
173. **Platonic-style Euler equation 1/p + 1/q = 1/2 + 1/E as the 2-term cousin** [`analogues-0173`; low/cheap] — Regular maps {p,q} satisfy 1/p + 1/q − 1/2 = χ/(2E). Two-term Egyptian equations arise from Euler's formula; ES is the analogous three-type (hypermap) equation. — *First step:* Context only; record the hypermap equation N/x + N/y + N/z − N = χ as the general form.
174. **Hypergeometric differential equations: exponent differences 1/x, 1/y, 1/z with Σ = 4/n** [`analogues-0174`; low/cheap] — Schwarz's list: the hypergeometric equation with exponent differences (λ, μ, ν) has monodromy a triangle group when they are reciprocals of integers; λ + μ + ν < 1 gives hyperbolic monodromy. ES ⇔ some Schwarz triangle with reciprocal angles has angle sum 4π/n. — *First step:* Context; check whether any ES triple gives an arithmetic monodromy group (overlaps Takeuchi item).
175. **Weighted projective planes P(a,b,c) and Egyptian conditions for Fano/Kähler–Einstein** [`analogues-0175`; low/medium] — Well-formedness and Fano conditions for P(a,b,c) and for hypersurfaces in weighted projective space are linear/Egyptian conditions on weights (e.g. Σ w_i > d for Fano hypersurfaces). Reid's 95 K3 families arise from such equations. — *First step:* Look for weighted hypersurface conditions of the form Σ 1/w_i = r (equality) in Reid's/Iano-Fletcher's lists; match with 4/n.
176. **Markov/Hacking–Prokhorov: degenerations of P² ↔ Markov triples; ES surface as an analogous 'mutation' equation** [`analogues-0176`; med/cheap] — Markov triples a² + b² + c² = 3abc classify degenerations of P² to P(a², b², c²). ES's surface 4xyz = n(xy + yz + zx) is a cubic with Vieta-type involutions on each coordinate (it is linear in each variable). — *First step:* Check: 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) is linear in x, so x is determined by (y,z) — there is no second root, hence no Vieta involution; record this negative and look for another birational automorphism.
177. **Birational automorphism group of the ES surface S_n** [`analogues-0177`; med/cheap] — S_n: 4xyz = n(xy + yz + zx) ⇔ (after 1/x = X etc.) the plane X + Y + Z = 4/n, a linear plane; integrality is what makes it hard. The 'hidden' automorphisms preserving integrality are the Type I/II reparametrizations. — *First step:* List all integral-structure-preserving maps among Type I/II parametrizations and check for maps with n' ≠ n (scaling, Möbius in parameters).
178. **Apollonian/Descartes: curvatures with reciprocal relations** [`analogues-0178`; high/cheap] — Descartes' theorem relates curvatures quadratically; Apollonian packings carry orbit structure (thin groups) with local–global principles (Bourgain–Kontorovich density one; failures found by Haag–Kertzer–Rickards–Stange). ES's reciprocal-sum structure is linear in curvatures 1/x. — *First step:* Read Haag–Kertzer–Rickards–Stange (local-global failures in Apollonian packings) and compare their reciprocity obstruction with T1 at odd squares.
179. **Ford circles / Farey: 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/n as a tangency/curvature condition** [`analogues-0179`; high/cheap] — Farey neighbours and Ford circles encode 1/(qq') differences; three unit fractions summing to 4/n can be read as a chain of Farey steps. The repo's Farey/forest forms are instances. — *First step:* Pointer only; check BRAINSTORM/farey_ford_cf.md.
180. **Egyptian fractions in the Sierpiński triangle / Pascal mod 2** [`analogues-0180`; low/cheap] — Recent work connects Egyptian fractions to the Sierpiński triangle (De Carli et al.). A 2-adic/Lucas-theorem structure might organize 4/n representations by binary digits of n. — *First step:* Read arXiv:2412.09728 to see the precise correspondence and test whether ES solution counts correlate with binary digit patterns of p.
181. **Cluster algebras / friezes: unit fractions from Conway–Coxeter friezes** [`analogues-0181`; high/cheap] — Friezes encode continued fractions and SL₂ words; ES₅/SL₂-word forms suggest a frieze pattern of width ≤ 3 that produces 4/p. The repo has FRIEZE_ES. — *First step:* Pointer only; read FRIEZE_ES.md for status.
182. **Tropical ES: min(−v(x), −v(y), −v(z)) structure and Newton polytopes** [`analogues-0182`; high/cheap] — Tropicalizing 4xyz − n(xy + yz + zx) at a prime ℓ gives a tropical surface; ES solutions with given ℓ-adic valuations lie on cells of it. Over each ℓ | n the cell structure forces which denominators carry ℓ. — *First step:* Compute the tropical variety of the ES surface for ℓ = 2 and ℓ = p and list all cells; match with Type I/II and with the 2-adic observations (m = 8, 4 | denominator).
183. **Min-plus 'ES': n/4 = min-plus harmonic combination — degenerate, records the archimedean bound** [`analogues-0183`; med/cheap] — Tropicalizing at ∞ (log-sizes) gives max(−log x, −log y, −log z) = log(4/n) up to O(1): just the size bound x ≍ n. So the tropical-at-∞ world only records sizes, confirming that the archimedean information is the size window. — *First step:* Context lemma; no computation needed.
184. **Squared rectangles: 4/n via Kirchhoff networks with three parallel branches of integer conductance** [`analogues-0184`; med/cheap] — Brooks–Smith–Stone–Tutte: a squared rectangle corresponds to a planar network with currents = square sizes. Three parallel branches each a series of identical resistors give the strip-tiling item; richer networks give 'generalized ES'. — *First step:* Enumerate 2-terminal series–parallel networks with ≤ 4 integer resistors and determine which give every n/4.
185. **Series–parallel networks with k unit resistors realize which rationals? ES as the 3-branch case** [`analogues-0185`; low/cheap] — The set of resistances of series–parallel networks of k unit resistors is a classical sequence (OEIS). A 3-branch parallel with integer resistors is an ES triple; the general series-parallel set is much larger. — *First step:* Look up the OEIS sequence for 'number of distinct resistances with n unit resistors (series–parallel)' and its structural results.
186. **Probability: 1/x + 1/y + 1/z as the rate of the minimum of three exponentials** [`analogues-0186`; low/cheap] — If T_i ~ Exp(mean x_i) are independent, min T_i has mean 1/Σ(1/x_i). ES ⇔ the minimum of three exponential clocks with integer means has mean n/4. Equivalent for discrete clocks: the first success among three periodic processes. — *First step:* Low priority; note.
187. **Gauss–Bonnet for polygons: 4/n as total angle deficit of an integer-angle triangle** [`analogues-0187`; low/cheap] — A Euclidean/hyperbolic triangle with angles π/x, π/y, π/z has angle sum 4π/n exactly when ES holds; Gauss–Bonnet gives area π(1 − 4/n). Same as triangle orbifold item, but useful for geometric constructions (gluing triangles). — *First step:* Explore: if ES(n₁) and ES(n₂) triangles glue along an edge, what Egyptian equation does the quadrilateral satisfy?
188. **Lens spaces / Dedekind sums attached to ES triples** [`analogues-0188`; low/medium] — Seifert spaces from ES triples have Casson–Walker and Reidemeister torsion invariants expressed through Dedekind sums s(1, x_i). Dedekind sums satisfy reciprocity, a possible source of T1-like constraints. — *First step:* Compute Σ s(1, x_i) (or the Casson–Walker invariant) for ES triples at small p and look for congruences mod small numbers.
189. **Integral fusion rings of rank 4 with Egyptian dimension equations (Alekseyev–Bruns–Dong)** [`analogues-0189`; med/cheap] — Classification of integral Grothendieck rings and modular data uses Egyptian-fraction equations with constraints, solved by computer to high rank. Their algorithms enumerate Egyptian solutions under divisibility constraints efficiently. — *First step:* Read the algorithm sections of arXiv:2507.07023 and arXiv:2302.01613; assess reuse for ES censuses.
190. **Toric/polytope view: ES triples ↔ reflexive-like triangles with given lattice data** [`analogues-0190`; med/cheap] — A lattice triangle with vertices on axes at distances x, y, z (simplex with intercepts) defines the plane X/x + Y/y + Z/z = 1, which contains the diagonal point (t,t,t) iff Σ 1/x_i = 1/t. So ES ⇔ some plane with positive integer intercepts passes through (n/4, n/4, n/4). — *First step:* Formalize: planes with integer intercepts through (t,t,t), t = n/4; parametrize by normal vector (1/x, 1/y, 1/z) and relate to the repo's lattice forms.

### E. Logic, random models, q-deformations, cross-world data

191. **ES is false in a model of open induction (via Mordell–Schinzel in a discretely ordered ring)** [`analogues-0191`; med/medium] — Discretely ordered rings like Z[T] with T infinitely large (and Shepherdson-type models of IOpen built from Puiseux polynomials) are models of weak arithmetic. ES in Z[T] with this order is the eventual-positivity polynomial world, where Mordell–Schinzel rules out n = mT + r². — *First step:* Check that a suitable ring (e.g. Shepherdson's model, or Z + T·Q[T] variants) satisfies IOpen and that the Mordell–Schinzel argument applies there (denominators may have rational non-constant coefficients).
192. **ES is a Π₁ sentence: bounded search, so independence from PA would imply truth** [`analogues-0192`; high/cheap] — With x ≤ y ≤ z, x ≤ 3n/4 and z ≤ n²-ish bounds (explicit poly(n)), ES is ∀n ∃(bounded) — Π⁰₁. Any counterexample is a standard integer; models of PA where ES fails contain a nonstandard counterexample. — *First step:* Write the explicit bound on z in terms of n (from 1/z ≥ 4/n − 2/y …) and record the Π₁ form; check BRAINSTORM/logic_* memos for prior discussion.
193. **ES in models of IΔ₀: does bounded arithmetic prove 'almost all n'?** [`analogues-0193`; low/cheap] — Vaughan's density theorem uses analytic number theory; formalizing it in weak arithmetic is unlikely, but elementary 'almost-all' proofs (sieve-free covering arguments) might live in IΔ₀ + Ω₁. — *First step:* Survey: is there any Erdős–Straus-type density statement formalized in bounded arithmetic? (Probably not — low priority.)
194. **Ultraproduct of Z/pZ? No — ultraproduct of Z[1/S_k] with growing S: ES transfers by Łoś** [`analogues-0194`; high/cheap] — Since ES holds over every Z[1/ℓ] (odd ℓ < 3000 checked), it holds in ultraproducts of these rings; but these ultraproducts are not Z. Łoś only transfers first-order sentences true in almost all factors, giving nothing for Z. — *First step:* Record the negative; double-check that 'positive' is first-order definable in Z[1/ℓ] (it is, via sums of four squares).
195. **Beurling generalized integers: build a system where some generalized prime fails ES** [`analogues-0195`; med/medium] — ES's Type II needs divisors of the additive shift 4Cp + 1; Beurling systems keep multiplicative structure but destroy additive structure. In a Beurling system with integers 'close to' ℕ (Diamond–Montgomery–Vorhauer type), ES may fail infinitely often. — *First step:* Define ES for Beurling integers N_P (with an addition borrowed from R), construct a random Beurling system and test ES for its primes numerically.
196. **Random-set analogue: replace '4Cp + 1' by a random integer of the same size and test ES-type existence** [`analogues-0196`; high/cheap] — The lottery model treats divisors of 4Cp + 1 as random. Simulating with genuinely random integers N_C ≈ 4Cp gives the 'random world' where ES holds with probability → 1 but fails sometimes. — *First step:* Simulate: for random 'p' replace 4Cp + 1 by uniform random integers in [4Cp, 4Cp + 4C·p^{0.5}] and measure failure frequency at p ~ 10^6.
197. **Cramér-type model for 'hard primes': which properties of p predict few solutions?** [`analogues-0197`; high/cheap] — In the computation, the primes with fewest solutions are 5, 13, 17, 193, 29, 41, 73, 97. Hard primes may be those with p − 1 or p + 3 having few small factors (fewer Type I/II options). — *First step:* Regress #solutions(p) for p < 2·10^4 on ω(p+3), ω((p+1)/2), smoothness of p − 1, etc.
198. **q-deformed ES: [4]_q/[n]_q = 1/[x]_q + 1/[y]_q + 1/[z]_q in Q(q)** [`analogues-0198`; low/cheap] — With q-integers [k]_q = (1 − q^k)/(1 − q), at q = 1 this is ES. In Q(q) the equation is extremely rigid (cyclotomic factorizations), so solutions are probably rare or absent. — *First step:* Search x, y, z ≤ 60, n ≤ 60 for exact identities in Q(q) using polynomial arithmetic.
199. **q-deformed rationals (Morier-Genoud–Ovsienko) and the continued-fraction form ES₅** [`analogues-0199`; low/medium] — q-deformed rationals [a/b]_q are defined via continued fractions; ES₅ characterizes ES via continued-fraction length. A q-ES₅ statement could be stated for [4/p]_q and tested for positivity of coefficients. — *First step:* Check whether Morier-Genoud–Ovsienko 'q-deformed rationals and q-continued fractions' (Forum Math. Sigma 2020) defines sums; test [4/p]_q against sums of three q-unit fractions.
200. **Cross-world hard primes: 241 and 2521 fail in several constrained worlds** [`analogues-0200`; high/cheap] — 241 fails 'all even' (m = 8), 'a denominator ≡ 0 mod 4' and 'all denominators sums of two squares'; 2521 fails 'z = lcm' and 'sums of two squares'. Primes failing several strengthenings may be intrinsically hard for ES. — *First step:* Note 2521 = lcm(1,…,10) + 1 and 241 = 240 + 1 (240 = 2⁴·3·5); test whether p − 1 highly composite (many small factors) correlates with failing strengthenings.
201. **Highly composite p − 1 makes p hard? (2521 = lcm(1..10)+1, 241 = 240+1, 1801 = 1800+1, 601 = 600+1)** [`analogues-0201`; high/cheap] — Several failures of constrained worlds are primes with p − 1 very smooth (601, 1801, 2521, 241). If p − 1 has many small factors then p ≡ 1 modulo many small moduli, i.e. p lies in square classes (1 is a square) for all those moduli — exactly where T1-type obstructions bite. — *First step:* For p < 10^6, compute the largest M with p ≡ 1 mod M among smooth M and correlate with #solutions(p) and with constrained-world failures.
202. **No denominator ≡ 1 (mod 3): fails only at p = 5, 13, 37, 97 below 2·10^4** [`analogues-0202`; high/cheap] — Requiring all denominators to avoid the class 1 mod 3 fails at only four small primes. This 3-adic constrained world is almost as complete as ES. — *First step:* Classify the surviving solutions by their mod-3 pattern; check if one pattern (e.g. two denominators ≡ 0 mod 3) suffices for p > 97 up to 10^6.
203. **Size-capped ES: max denominator ≤ p²/8 fails at 45 primes below 2·10^4 (incl. 5, 13, 17, 29)** [`analogues-0203`; high/cheap] — The cap z ≤ p²/8 removes the largest solutions (Type II with z ≍ p²); 45 primes then fail. The failure set shows which primes depend on the 'extreme' solutions. — *First step:* Compute c(p) = min_solutions max(x,y,z)/p² for p < 2·10^4; check whether c(p) → 0 or stays bounded below for infinitely many p.
204. **Type II with x not divisible by p never fails below 2·10^4** [`analogues-0204`; high/cheap] — Solutions with p | y, p | z, p ∤ x exist for every p ≡ 1 mod 4 below 2·10^4. This is the 'pure Type II' strengthening (Elsholtz–Tao notation). — *First step:* Compare with the repo's existing Type II censuses (Z52_BANKED / I3 censuses) to avoid duplication; then count pure-Type-II solutions vs log²p.
205. **Probabilistic 'Schinzel world': random rationals a/b with b prime — what fraction are 3-term sums?** [`analogues-0205`; med/cheap] — Luca–Pappalardi/Mond–Portier give Σ_p A₃(p) ≍ x(log x)³; so a random numerator a ≤ p has probability ≍ (log p)³/p of being representable. ES says a = 4 always is: 4 is special because small numerators have more representations. — *First step:* Compute #representations of a/p as a function of a for fixed p ~ 10^4; fit decay in a.
206. **Dynamical world: Farey/Gauss map orbits of 4/p and 'three-step returns'** [`analogues-0206`; med/cheap] — ES₅ (length ≤ 3) asks for short orbits of a map on rationals. In the dynamical world, random rationals have orbit lengths ~ log p; ES needs a 'short-cut' orbit of length 3 for one of many starting points tied to p. — *First step:* Check repo's z31_dynamics_ergodic.md; compute the distribution of minimal ES₅ lengths over starting points for p ≤ 10^4.
207. **Computability world: ES for 'computable reals'/Turing degrees — category error check** [`analogues-0207`; high/cheap] — Considered: 'ES over computable reals' is meaningless (no integrality). Kept only the meaningful variant: ES restricted to n in a decidable set is decidable for each n, and the set of ES-failures is co-c.e. — *First step:* None (closed).
208. **Function-field random-matrix model applied over Z: Katz–Sarnak symmetry type of ES counts?** [`analogues-0208`; low/medium] — If the FF fixed-P ES count is a trace of a Frobenius on some cohomology (sum over Type II data), its fluctuations follow a symmetry type (U, Sp, O). Over Z the same symmetry type would predict lower-tail probabilities. — *First step:* Compute FF fixed-P counts for q = 3, deg P = 8, normalize, and compare histogram with Sato–Tate/semicircle/other Katz–Sarnak laws.
209. **Non-standard primes: ES at nonstandard p in a model of PA ⇒ lower-tail of counts** [`analogues-0209`; low/cheap] — In a nonstandard model, a counterexample would be a nonstandard prime with zero solutions; standard number theory (Vaughan-type density) holds in PA, so such p is 'generic'. Nothing transfers back, but the framing suggests stating ES failure as a statement about 'generic primes' (Hilbert-irreducibility-like). — *First step:* Low priority; note.
210. **ES for elements of Z_p (p-adic) with 'positivity' from an embedding into R — not well-defined** [`analogues-0210`; high/cheap] — Category-error check: Z_p has no archimedean embedding, so positivity cannot be imported; the meaningful p-adic analogues are local solubility (always) and p-adic cones (items in batch B). — *First step:* None (closed).
211. **Adelic counting: Tamagawa-type volume of ES integral points with bounded height** [`analogues-0211`; high/medium] — Integral points on the affine ES surface of height ≤ H should be ~ c·(log H)^r·H^a by a Hardy–Littlewood/Tamagawa heuristic; Bright–Loughran's no-BM result means no Brauer correction at all? (check whether their result is for integral or rational points). — *First step:* Read Bright–Loughran for the precise statement (integral BM) and compute the singular series at p for the ES surface; compare with actual solution counts.
212. **ES over F_q (finite fields) with a 'size' notion via lifting to [0, q): box-restricted solutions** [`analogues-0212`; med/medium] — Over F_q, 4/n = Σ 1/x_i trivially has solutions. Requiring representatives x_i ∈ [1, H] with H small (a box) gives the 'small solutions of congruences' world (Heath-Brown, Shparlinski style). — *First step:* Formulate: for M = p·(something), does 4xyz ≡ p(xy+yz+zx) mod M with x,y,z ≤ M^θ force equality? Then search the literature for small solutions of such congruences.
213. **Modular-hyperbola world: Type II as points on xy ≡ c (mod m) in a box** [`analogues-0213`; high/cheap] — Type II ES reduces to solving xy ≡ c (mod m) with x, y in specific intervals. The distribution of points on modular hyperbolas in boxes is controlled by Kloosterman sums (Shparlinski survey). — *First step:* Map one ES slice exactly to a modular-hyperbola box problem and compare required box size with the Weil-bound threshold.
214. **Numerator-8 and 4 | denominator coincidence: test an explicit bijection between the two solution sets** [`analogues-0214`; high/cheap] — Up to 2·10^4 both 'all denominators even' (⇔ 8/p) and 'some denominator ≡ 0 mod 4' fail exactly at {17, 241}. A map: a solution of 8/p (x', y', z') gives 4/p with (2x', 2y', 2z'); does every solution with 4 | x arise from some all-even solution and vice versa? — *First step:* For p < 2000, compute both solution sets and test whether 'has a solution with 4 | some denominator' ⇔ 'has an all-even solution' solution-by-solution (not just existence).
215. **ES in 'Z with a different order': positive cone = {n : n ≡ 1 mod 4 or …} is not multiplicatively closed — design check** [`analogues-0215`; high/cheap] — Orders on Z other than the usual one don't exist (Z has a unique ordering as an ordered ring). So 'other positivity on Z' must be a semigroup restriction (constraint worlds), not a new order. — *First step:* None (closed).
216. **Prime-power numerators: m = 4 = 2² vs m = 9, 25, 49 — do odd prime squares behave like 4?** [`analogues-0216`; med/cheap] — Divisor-closure: 9/p solvable ⇒ 3/p solvable (trivial). For m = ℓ², the 'hard part' is ℓ² itself. Compare exception sets for m = 9, 25 with ES. — *First step:* Compute exceptions of 9/n and 25/n (3 terms) for n ≤ 10^5; compare with Mordell-type identity coverage modulo 840·k.
217. **Gaussian-norm constrained world: failures are NOT explained by mod 8 or the quartic character of 2** [`analogues-0217`; high/cheap] — Failures of 'all denominators sums of two squares' below 2·10^4 (40 primes) occur in both classes 1 and 5 mod 8, in non-square classes mod 840 (e.g. 709, 829), and 17 of 40 have 2 as a quartic residue (vs 48% overall among p ≡ 1 mod 8). So no simple local/reciprocity explanation is visible. — *First step:* Compute the lottery-model expected number of norm-constrained solutions per p (densities of sums of two squares among Type I/II denominators) and compare predicted with observed failure frequency.
218. **Chain world (x | y | z): every failure is ≡ 1 (mod 24), and 161 of the 267 such primes fail** [`analogues-0218`; high/cheap] — All 161 chain-world failures below 2·10^4 lie in the class p ≡ 1 mod 24 (the square class of (Z/24)^*), but mod 120 and mod 840 they spread over non-square classes (e.g. 73 ≡ 3 mod 5). So the chain world has a T1-type square-class obstruction at modulus 24 plus a lottery component inside that class. — *First step:* Prove: chain solutions exist for all p ≡ 5, 13, 17 (mod 24) via explicit identities; then study the density of chain-solvable p within p ≡ 1 mod 24 as p grows.

### F. Sibling problems with known status (step that works → integer statement for ES)

219. **xy + yz + zx = N (Borwein–Choi): a symmetric ternary problem solved up to one GRH-exception** [`analogues-0219`; high/cheap] — Borwein–Choi determine the N not of the form xy + yz + zx (x, y, z ≥ 1) — a finite list related to idoneal numbers, complete under GRH up to one possible extra value — via class numbers of Q(√−N). For an ES solution, xy + yz + zx = 4xyz/n (the pretzel determinant). — *First step:* Write ES as 'xy + yz + zx = N with the extra constraint xyz = nN/4' and check whether the Borwein–Choi form correspondence keeps track of xyz.
220. **Idoneal numbers and ES: N = xy + yz + zx failing ⇔ class group of discriminant −4N is 2-torsion** [`analogues-0220`; med/medium] — Euler's idoneal numbers are exactly those where the class group is elementary 2-abelian; representations by xy+yz+zx relate to this. ES might be reformulated as a statement about elements of order > 2 in class groups of discriminants tied to p. — *First step:* Derive, from an ES solution, a binary form of discriminant −4N (N = 4xyz/p) and identify its class; test whether non-2-torsion is forced.
221. **Ternary quadratic forms (Duke–Schulze-Pillot): local ⇒ global except spinor exceptions ↔ T1** [`analogues-0221`; high/cheap] — Large integers locally represented by a positive ternary form are represented, except finitely many spinor square classes (ineffective via Siegel). T1 at odd squares is ES's analogue of a spinor exception: a square-class phenomenon that blocks a uniform method but not the truth. — *First step:* Read THREE_SQUARES.md / z31_quadratic_forms.md for prior attempts; check whether some ES slice is exactly a ternary representation problem.
222. **Gauss–Legendre three squares: the local obstruction 4^a(8b+7) vs ES having none** [`analogues-0222`; high/cheap] — Three squares has a local obstruction and is otherwise always solvable (via genus theory/class numbers). ES has no local obstruction (Bright–Loughran) — so if ES were a 'genus-theoretic' problem it would be always solvable for elementary reasons. — *First step:* Context; see THREE_SQUARES.md.
223. **Sums of three cubes (Booker–Sutherland): cubic surfaces with integral points, heuristics vs truth** [`analogues-0223`; high/cheap] — x³ + y³ + z³ = k is a cubic surface with a local obstruction (k ≡ ±4 mod 9) and Heath-Brown's heuristic predicts infinitely many solutions otherwise; ES is a cubic surface too, with no local obstruction and polylog expected count at fixed n. — *First step:* Compare expected-count heuristics: Heath-Brown's for three cubes vs log²p for ES; note no proof technique exists in either world for pointwise existence.
224. **Ternary Goldbach (proved) vs binary Goldbach (open): where ES sits** [`analogues-0224`; high/cheap] — Ternary problems with power-size expected counts are proved by the circle method; binary ones are open. ES at fixed p has expected count ≍ log²p, smaller than binary Goldbach's ≍ p/log²p — ES is 'sub-binary', so circle-method-type methods are not expected to work pointwise. — *First step:* Context; record the comparison of expected counts in the memo header.
225. **Graham's theorem: every integer > 77 is a sum of distinct integers whose reciprocals sum to 1** [`analogues-0225`; med/cheap] — Graham (1963) proved this via explicit constructions plus induction (splitting). It is a 'many terms' Egyptian existence theorem with an exceptional set (≤ 77) computed exactly. — *First step:* Read Graham's proof; formulate the analogous splitting move for 3-term ES (none expected), and for 4-term versions with constraints.
226. **Croot's colouring theorem and Bloom's density theorem: Egyptian existence in dense sets** [`analogues-0226`; high/cheap] — Croot proved that any finite colouring of ℕ has a monochromatic set with reciprocal sum 1; Bloom proved that sets of positive upper density contain such sets. The method (Fourier analysis on smooth numbers, many terms) fails for 3 terms. — *First step:* Check Liu–Sawhney 'further questions' for bounded-length results with dense denominators.
227. **Conlon–Fox–He on an Erdős–Graham question about Egyptian fractions** [`analogues-0227`; med/cheap] — Recent work resolves an Erdős–Graham question on Egyptian fractions (details to read). It belongs to the modern 'Egyptian existence' toolkit along with Bloom and Liu–Sawhney. — *First step:* Read arXiv:2404.16016 abstract and main theorem; note the technique.
228. **Znám's problem (solved for all k ≥ 5): Egyptian equations with divisibility constraints** [`analogues-0228`; med/cheap] — Znám's problem asks for sets where each element properly divides the product of the others plus one; equivalent to Egyptian equations Σ 1/x_i + 1/Π x_i = 1. Existence for all k ≥ 5 is known (Sun Qi); k = 2..4 have none. — *First step:* Check Znám/Sun Qi constructions for an adaptable gadget giving numerator 4.
229. **Agoh–Giuga and Egyptian divisibility: Σ 1/p_i − 1/Π p_i ∈ ℤ** [`analogues-0229`; low/cheap] — Giuga numbers satisfy Σ_{p|n} 1/p − 1/n ∈ ℤ. Egyptian equations over prime denominators with a correction term are another sibling with open status (Agoh–Giuga conjecture). — *First step:* Low priority; read a survey on Giuga numbers for techniques on Egyptian equations with prime denominators.
230. **Odd perfect numbers and abundancy: Σ_{d | n} 1/d = 2 as an Egyptian constraint** [`analogues-0230`; low/cheap] — σ(n)/n = Σ_{d|n} 1/d; perfect numbers solve an Egyptian equation with denominators forced to be all divisors. Bounds on odd perfect numbers (Nielsen) use unit-fraction inequalities. — *First step:* Low priority: note as sibling.
231. **Harmonic numbers' p-adic valuations (Boyd) and the integrality of Σ 1/x** [`analogues-0231`; low/cheap] — Boyd's conjecture: J_p = {n : p | numerator(H_n)} is finite; studied via p-adic trees. ES at p is a p-adic statement about which unit-fraction sums have valuation −1 at p. — *First step:* Low priority; read Boyd's 'A p-adic study of the partial sums of the harmonic series' for tree technique.
232. **Least quadratic non-residue (Burgess/Vinogradov) ↔ least ES certificate** [`analogues-0232`; high/cheap] — ES certificates are found by searching small parameters (e.g. least C with 4Cp + 1 having a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C). The least quadratic non-residue problem has a GRH bound O(log² p) and unconditional p^{1/(4√e)}. — *First step:* Compute the least certificate parameter C(p) for p ≤ 10^7 and compare its growth with log² p; check EXSET_LINNIK.md.
233. **Ford's divisors-in-intervals H(x, y, 2y) with a congruence condition** [`analogues-0233`; high/medium] — Ford determined the order of the number of n ≤ x having a divisor in (y, 2y]. ES slices need a divisor of a p-tied integer in a window AND a residue class — a congruence-restricted Ford problem. — *First step:* Check whether 'divisors in intervals and residue classes' has been treated (search Ford, Hall–Tenenbaum 'Divisors', congruence restrictions).
234. **Hooley's Δ-function and concentration of divisors ↔ the lottery's 'ticket clumping'** [`analogues-0234`; med/medium] — Hooley's Δ(n) = max_u #{d | n : u < d ≤ eu}. Divisors clumping in short ranges reduces the effective number of independent tickets in the ES lottery. — *First step:* Check Hall–Tenenbaum results on Δ on average and adapt to the family {4Cp + 1 : C ≤ C₀}.
235. **Erdős multiplication-table problem ↔ number of distinct products in Type II parametrizations** [`analogues-0235`; low/medium] — Ford's resolution of the multiplication-table problem counts distinct products ab ≤ x. ES Type II parameters generate integers as products; overlaps among products reduce effective tickets. — *First step:* Compute the overlap rate among Type II certificate products for fixed p and compare with Ford's constant.
236. **Covering systems: Hough's minimum modulus theorem ↔ impossibility of finite ES coverings** [`analogues-0236`; high/cheap] — Hough proved that distinct-moduli covering systems have bounded minimum modulus; the Balister et al. distortion method strengthens this. ES finite coverings by certificate classes fail at square classes (Mordell). Both are 'covering obstruction' theorems. — *First step:* Read BRAINSTORM/covering_distortion_dual.md for the state; formulate the ES covering as a covering system with moduli 4C.
237. **Apollonian local–global failure (Haag–Kertzer–Rickards–Stange): a reciprocity obstruction removing an infinite thin set** [`analogues-0237`; high/cheap] — HKRS proved the Apollonian local-global conjecture is false: quadratic/quartic reciprocity obstructions remove infinite families of curvatures. T1 at odd squares is a reciprocity obstruction removing certificate families (not solutions). — *First step:* Read the Annals paper's obstruction section and write the analogy table: orbit ↔ certificate family, missing residues ↔ T1 squares.
238. **Zaremba's conjecture (Bourgain–Kontorovich density one; Huang; Shkredov–Moshchevitin) ↔ ES₅** [`analogues-0238`; high/cheap] — Zaremba: every q has a/q with bounded partial quotients; Bourgain–Kontorovich proved density one via thin-orbit counting. ES₅: ES ⇔ λ(p) ≤ 3 continued-fraction length form. Thin-orbit methods give almost-all, as for ES. — *First step:* Pointer to ZAREMBA_TRANSFER.md.
239. **Markoff surfaces: strong approximation for almost all primes (Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak, W. Chen)** [`analogues-0239`; high/medium] — For Markoff, the integral points mod p form a single orbit except for a small set of p, proven for all large p by W. Chen via a divisibility argument (degree of the mod-p orbit). ES has no Vieta group, but a different group action on its integral points could play the same role. — *First step:* Find any group acting on ES integral points or on certificate data mod p with orbit-size divisibility; see MARKOFF_ES.md.
240. **Lehmer's totient problem: Egyptian-type constraints ∏(1 − 1/p) from φ(n) | n − 1** [`analogues-0240`; low/cheap] — φ(n) | n − 1 implies inequalities and Egyptian-type relations on the prime factors. Another rigid multiplicative/Egyptian sibling with open status. — *First step:* Low priority.
241. **Primes of the form x² + ny² and genus theory ↔ certificate families as representations** [`analogues-0241`; high/medium] — Type II certificates at p are representations p = (something)·(something) − (something), close to binary forms. Cox's theory of p = x² + ny² (ring class fields) gives exact Chebotarev descriptions. — *First step:* Search for certificate families whose condition is a binary-form representation of p (not a congruence); NONCONG_LIFTS.md may have candidates.
242. **Friedlander–Iwaniec / Heath-Brown thin-polynomial primes ↔ ES-good primes in thin sets** [`analogues-0242`; low/cheap] — Primes of the form x² + y⁴ (FI) and x³ + 2y³ (HB) are proved infinite by sieve methods with bilinear forms. ES-good certificates for thin sets of p might be proved similarly — but ES needs ALL p. — *First step:* Low priority; note.
243. **Erdős–Selfridge/Graham 'Egyptian fractions with denominators in [N, cN]' as size-window sibling** [`analogues-0243`; med/cheap] — Problems asking for Σ 1/x_i = 1 with all x_i in a dyadic range relate to ES solutions whose denominators are confined to windows (p/4 < x ≤ 3p/4 etc.). — *First step:* Pointer: compare with Croot's short-interval result (batch C).
244. **Sierpiński's 5/n, Schinzel's m/n: almost-all results (Vaughan) are uniform in m — what uniformity is known?** [`analogues-0244`; med/cheap] — Vaughan's density result covers every fixed m. The dependence of the exceptional-set bound on m is the quantitative sibling link between ES and its numerator neighbours. — *First step:* Read Vaughan 1970 for m-dependence; record.
245. **Representation of 1 by k unit fractions: Sylvester/Curtiss bound and maximal denominators** [`analogues-0245`; med/cheap] — The largest denominator in Σ_{i≤k} 1/x_i = 1 is bounded doubly exponentially (Curtiss/Kellogg; Ambro–Barcau sharp bound for rationals). For ES the largest denominator is ≤ poly(n). — *First step:* Read arXiv:1412.3263 for their sharp bound specialized to 4/n with 3 terms.
246. **Counting Egyptian fractions (Bettin–Grenié–Molteni): number of k-term representations of 1** [`analogues-0246`; med/cheap] — Precise asymptotics/lower bounds for the number of k-term Egyptian representations exist; ES counts (Elsholtz–Tao) are the numerator-4 three-term analogue. — *First step:* Read arXiv:1906.11986 / 2509.10030 for methods; compare with Elsholtz–Tao's average counts.
247. **Ternary Egyptian fractions with prime denominator: A₃(p) upper bound x(log x)³(log log x)² (Mond–Portier)** [`analogues-0247`; high/cheap] — Mond–Portier sharpen Luca–Pappalardi's upper bound on Σ A₃(p). Their method counts numerators per prime via the Type I/II parametrization and divisor sums. — *First step:* Read 2201.11805 and check whether their method yields a lower bound for the number of m ≡ 0 (mod 4) in M(p) on average over p.
248. **Huang–Vaughan mean value theorems for binary Egyptian fractions** [`analogues-0248`; med/cheap] — Mean values of the number of representations a/n = 1/x + 1/y over n (and a) are known with secondary terms. These are the 2-term building blocks of ES slices. — *First step:* Read arXiv:1108.0096 / 1109.2274 for the error terms; see if they allow a correlation estimate across a.
249. **Lattice-point/hyperbola methods (Dirichlet divisor problem) for fixed-p ES counts** [`analogues-0249`; med/cheap] — ES counts at fixed p are sums of divisor-counting functions over arithmetic progressions; the Dirichlet hyperbola method with exponent pairs gives error terms. — *First step:* Write the fixed-p count as a lattice-point count under a hyperbola with congruences and identify the error term size.
250. **Erdős–Straus vs 'every prime p ≡ 1 mod 4 is a sum of two squares': constructive analogues** [`analogues-0250`; high/cheap] — Fermat's two-squares theorem has several proofs (Zagier's one-sentence involution, Thue's lemma pigeonhole, Gaussian integers). The repo's WINDMILL work transfers the involution proof. Thue's lemma (pigeonhole on a·x ≡ y) is another transferable template. — *First step:* Formulate a bilinear Thue-type pigeonhole for xy ≡ c (mod m) with box constraints and check whether it gives ES slices (repo LONGSHOT_PIGEONHOLE).
251. **Waring-type 'every n is a sum of three triangular numbers' (Gauss) ↔ ES via genus theory** [`analogues-0251`; med/cheap] — Gauss's Eureka theorem follows from three squares. Problems equivalent to ternary quadratic representability are 'easy'; ES's equation 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) is cubic. A quadratic slice (fixing one variable) gives binary problems. — *First step:* Context; check whether 'union over x of binary-form problems' has a ternary-form encoding (cf. Borwein–Choi item).
252. **Primitive prime divisors (Zsigmondy/Bang) as the integer replacement for 'units' in proved worlds** [`analogues-0252`; high/cheap] — In Z[1/ℓ] the universal divisor comes from 1 + ℓ^k; Zsigmondy guarantees new prime factors of a^k ± 1. Over Z the corresponding p-tied integers (4Cp + 1) have no such algebraic factor structure. — *First step:* List ES certificate families involving p^k ± 1 or similar (power ladders); check POWER_LADDER_ES.md for the state of the art.
253. **Artin's primitive root conjecture (Hooley under GRH) ↔ 'some ℓ has 1+ℓ^k with a 3 mod 4 factor'** [`analogues-0253`; med/cheap] — The Z[1/ℓ] mechanism needs η = ℓ^k with ℓ^k ≡ −1 mod e for some e ≡ 3 mod 4: an order condition on ℓ modulo e. Hooley-type GRH arguments control such order conditions for almost all ℓ. — *First step:* Prove unconditionally via the reciprocity argument (failure forces ℓ ≡ 1 mod 8) plus a choice of k; no GRH needed.
254. **Chebotarev-in-short-ranges (Lagarias–Odlyzko, Thorner–Zaman) for certificate fields** [`analogues-0254`; med/cheap] — If ES certificates at p correspond to p splitting in one of a family of number fields K_C (C ≤ C₀), ES ⇔ every p splits in some K_C with C small. Effective Chebotarev bounds give least primes splitting, not 'every prime splits somewhere'. — *First step:* Pointer: formulate ES as a Chebotarev covering problem and list the fields K_C for small C.
255. **Hilbert irreducibility / thin sets (Serre): ES failures must lie in a thin set?** [`analogues-0255`; med/medium] — Each Type II certificate family gives a polynomial-in-parameters set of good p; a counterexample p must avoid all of them. By Hilbert irreducibility style reasoning, the set of p avoiding a single family of positive density is 'thin-complement'. A union over growing families is the issue. — *First step:* Check whether the complement of a single Type I family is thin in Serre's sense; then whether countable unions preserve useful bounds.
256. **Andrews–Dyson-type partition identities as 'identities in growing families'** [`analogues-0256`; low/cheap] — Partition theory has infinite families of identities (Rogers–Ramanujan type) with growing parameters, proved by q-series. ES needs growing certificate families whose union covers all p; q-series identity machinery (Bailey chains) generates infinite families systematically. — *First step:* Low priority; look for an ES identity family indexed by k with a recursive (chain) structure, e.g. from power ladders.
257. **Unit equations (Evertse; S-unit theorem) ↔ the S-integer proved world** [`analogues-0257`; med/cheap] — Positive ES over Z[1/S] uses S-units; the finiteness of S-unit equation solutions (a + b = c in S-units) bounds the number of 'universal divisor' mechanisms available, explaining why each Z[1/ℓ] needs specific k. — *First step:* Write the S-unit equation underlying Lemma 3.1 (e·κ = 1 + η) and check what finiteness implies for fixed S.
